query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A surface fluorination treatment (e.g., spraying a dilute NaF aqueous solution) applied to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will induce formation of a thin, adherent, mixed refractory oxide scale (composed primarily of HfO2, Ta2O5, and TiO2) that dramatically slows subsequent oxygen ingress during high‐temperature exposure without degrading the alloy’s intrinsic mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled surface treatment by spraying a dilute NaF-containing aqueous solution onto the as-cast alloy, followed by a brief isothermal hold at 1000 °C to promote formation of a continuous, protective oxide scale.
generation.conditions: Exposure at 1000 °C in air for 100 hours (or similar high-temperature regime relevant for practical applications), with mechanical loading either in standard tensile tests at room temperature or at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a coherent, dense oxide scale that is enriched in refractory oxides (e.g., HfO2, Ta2O5, TiO2) mediated by a fluorine-induced surface reaction.
generation.mechanism: The NaF treatment modifies the surface chemistry so that, upon subsequent high-temperature exposure, fluorinated species (such as volatile metal fluorides) are formed and removed, leaving behind a stable and adherent oxide layer. This layer acts as an effective diffusion barrier which limits oxygen ingress while having minimal impact on the bulk microstructure and mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the fluorine-treated alloy will show a substantially reduced oxidation weight gain (e.g., on the order of an 80–90% reduction) during high-temperature exposure and will retain its useful tensile ductility and yield strength.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibits poor oxidation resistance (rapid oxide scale growth in air at 1000 °C) although its mechanical performance is acceptable.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective as long as the fluorine treatment is applied only to the surface (without altering bulk composition) and under high-temperature oxidizing conditions similar to 1000 °C in air with exposure times up to 100 hours; performance under significantly different environments or long-term cyclic thermal exposures remains to be verified.
generation.uncertainty: While fluorine treatment was shown to dramatically improve oxidation resistance in Ti-Al-Nb alloys (PMC9030595, sections 'Abstract' and 'Conclusions'), the direct extension of this method to a refractory HfNbTaTiZr alloy is not yet experimentally validated. Uncertainty arises from the difference in alloy chemistry (absence of Al) and the possible differences in the oxide scale composition and adherence. Thus, the specific constituents of the protective oxide film and their long-term stability may vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples. One set receives the fluorine (NaF) spray treatment followed by a short isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C to form the protective scale; the control set is left untreated. Both sets are then exposed to a high-temperature air environment at 1000 °C for 100 hours. After exposure, measure the oxidation weight gain and perform mechanical tensile tests (both room-temperature and 1000 °C at strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹). Surface analyses (e.g., SEM/EDS, XRD) should be conducted to characterize the oxide scale.
measurements: Oxidation weight gain per unit area
Microstructural integrity and adhesion of the oxide scale (via SEM/EDS)
Room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fluorine-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant (e.g., >70–80% reduction) decrease in oxidation weight gain relative to controls, or if the mechanical properties (ductility and yield strength) are adversely affected (e.g., reduced tensile ductility below the baseline 8–16% or yield strength falling well outside the 163–530 MPa range at 1000 °C), then the hypothesis is falsified.

In-depth analyses of the anti-oxidation behavior and structure of γ-TiAl alloys are of great significant for their maintenance and repair in engineering applications. In this work, fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys and fluorine-treated oxidized specimens with artificial defects were prepared by isothermal oxidation treatment at 1000 °C. Several characterization methods, including SEM, EDS, XRD and TEM, were used to evaluate the surface microstructure of the fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys and fluorine-treated oxidized specimens with artificial defects. The results indicate that the fluorine promoted the formation of an outer protective film of Al2O3, which significantly improved the oxidation resistance. The microcracks of oxidized specimens with the artificial defects provided a rapid diffusion passage for Ti and O elements during the 1000 °C/2 h isothermal oxidation treatment process, resulting in the quick growth of TiO2 toward the outside. The fine Al2O3 constituted a continuous film after the 1000 °C/100 h isothermal oxidation treatment. In this study, we executed a simple and effective strategy involving a two-step spraying and oxidation process to produce Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys with a dense Al2O3 film for application at high temperatures. The main results are as follows: (1)The oxidation resistance was significantly improved due to the formation of a protective Al2O3 film induced by the fluorine effect during isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C (6.03 mg/cm2 weight gain for the bare Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys, but 0.81 mg/cm2 for the fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys).(2)The Ti diffused along the artificial microcracks, resulting in a quick growth of TiO2 in a short time (2 h), while a continuous Al2O3 film was generated underneath the oxide scale during further isothermal oxidation (100 h).(3)The Al2O3 particles between the alloy and continuous Al2O3 film were reflected in the γ-TiAl and α2-Ti3Al phases, which improved the adhesion of the oxide scale (fluorine-treated specimen had a deep yellow oxide scale on the surface without any exfoliation). These findings represent significant progress towards reducing the high temperature oxidation resistance of TiAl intermetallics by surface fluorine modification.
